accuracy.evidence: Checked against NGSS MS-PS1-4 (adding or removing thermal energy changes particle motion and temperature) and the KS3 particle model and energy statements. Temperature is framed as a measure of average particle kinetic energy, not the speed of any one particle; kelvin conversion uses +273; absolute zero is described as lowest motion, not zero motion, to avoid the quantum objection; equilibrium of two identical blocks is exactly the mean only because the lab states it ignores losses to the air.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented alternative conceptions from Driver et al: particles expanding when heated (prediction bigger vs faster, challenge tag bigger), solid particles being still (prediction still vs vibrate, tag still), cold flowing into objects (tag cold), hotter always meaning more energy (cup vs bath sort and sparkler vs pool, tags total and spark), all particles sharing one speed (spread step, tag fastest), and the spoon overtaking the soup (tag over).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtemp is a thermometer-driven kinetic model: a live gas box whose particle speed scales with the square root of kelvin temperature, a freeze-frame with motion tails to pick out slow particles, a three-state motion matcher, a cup-versus-bath card sort and a two-block equilibrium press. Diffusion (flagdiff) only races spreading dye, so the gate measured shingle overlap under the 30 percent limit.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step does the idea rather than tells it: the learner heats to 100 C and cools to minus 20 C and watches the average kinetic energy bar move, taps three short-tailed particles in a frozen 100 C gas, places solid, liquid and gas motion cards, sorts five temperature or thermal energy statements, and presses 60/20 and 90/30 blocks together to watch both readouts converge on 40 and 60.

predictions.evidence: Three committed predictions before reveal: whether heated particles get bigger or faster, whether particles at one temperature all move at the same speed or have a mix, and whether particles in ice are still or vibrating. The equilibrium step asks for the shared temperature of 60 and 20 C blocks with 80, 40 and 20 as choices, and each reveal names why the wrong option fails.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The five-question challenge mixes food colouring in hot water, the sparkler versus pool energy comparison, ice at minus 10 C, a spoon in soup and the spread of speeds. Every wrong choice has its own tag and a hint that names the specific slip, for example cold does not flow, energy goes from the hotter soup, rather than a generic try again message.

readability.evidence: The pipeline readability gate passed for the learner audience: kid paragraphs use short sentences and define kinetic energy, average and thermal equilibrium in plain words, and the adult paragraphs stay within the 9.5 grade limit while still naming the KS3 terms kelvin, internal energy and thermal energy store that parents may want to look up.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no filler phrases and explanation overlap with lesson 317 Diffusion stayed under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph adds one new idea in order: motion in each state, heating and average kinetic energy, the spread of speeds, temperature versus total energy, and equilibrium between touching blocks.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 in both themes show the gas box and thermometer side by side, heat and cool buttons at full tap size, readable cup and bath cards with emoji, and the equilibrium blocks with clear readouts. Every drag (thermometer, cards, hot block) has a button twin such as Heat +20 C or Push the blocks together, so nothing needs precise dragging.

accessibility.evidence: The browser walk ran axe on desktop and phone in light and dark themes with zero violations and no console errors. The canvas carries an aria-label, every state change is spoken through the live region (temperature in C and kelvin, sorted counts, equilibrium readouts), colour is never the only cue because hot and cold blocks are labelled with temperatures.
